entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you worked very closely with Marv during 16 years?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, he was responsible to me for everything he did out there. And I was very, very fortunate, because Marv was so honest and so capable. I didn't have to supervise him too closely. Of course, I didn't have time, anyway. I'd go out there once a week, probably, and go around with him; and then he'd come in if he had problems in the office and we'd sit down and talk about it. It was a good relationship. When I retired, I told the dean, "You must appoint Marv as manager of that forest because he is so capable. He's so interested, and Marv thinks that's his forest, you know, and he handiles it just like it was his own." But he wouldn't make Marv fully responsible for it and responsible to him; he'd have to have somebody in the middle. So he put Beuter as Director of the Forest. Marv is responsible to Beuter, Beuter is responsible to the dean.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were really the director of the forest?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, director and manager.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did things change after Dean Stoltenberg became dean?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not much, because he didn't have much time to look at it, anyway, and he was not too knowledgeable in the management of Douglas-fir forests. He'd never had any experience or anything; left it pretty much up to me. He just kind of ignored it unless I came to him with some problem that I thought he ought to be in on, and help make the decision.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any activities that occurred in the forest that you haven't talked about?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: None that I can think of, but I remember thinking through the years that the forest is a true multiple-use forest. It's used for practically every use you can think of for a forest. Some of them a little conflicting, but most of them not conflicting. All of the things: timber
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: production, education, research, demonstration, recreation. We used to have quite a few show-me trips. When they would have their annual meeting, the forest service employees would want to come down and look and see what we were doing in a certain area of thinning or something. Demonstration type thing. We had people that would come from Europe to here, and they'd heard of Oregon State demonstration forest in Europe. When they come over here, they'd want to come out and see it. Just about every use of the forest you can think of. More uses probably than any one other forest in the state.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your own role in the history of the forest? What are you most proud of that you accomplished in your years of association?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if rm proud of any of it, but I think I started, really, the commercial use of the forest.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before you, they didn't really look at it from the standpoint of commercial harvest?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very little. Oh they cut a few trees here and there and so forth. They cut that one big clearcut just before I became manager - Dunn Forest - because they needed the money and it had been cut over once before. They went in and cut the trees that the first logger had left because they didn't figure they were merchantable; that's the only real cutting that was done. But when I became manager we set up a regular cutting budget and plan, and for years we cut nothing but thinning and salvage about 3.5 to 5 million, well 7 million the year of the blow down. Which can hardly be subtracted from the inventory. We set up another plan of going around once a year as soon as the dirt roads got dry in the spring and picking up every dead and downed tree on those two forests. Every one! Scout for them. Maybe it would be just one tree over here that had blown down in that winter; we'd pick that up and take it out. And the contractor made money, and we got stumpage out of it.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did you yard those out when you only had one? Did you go on horses?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, small cat, small tractors, and they had a portable loading machine, kind of, on a truck with a boom on it. They would just run that down the road, and what they'd do is two men would go out when we decided: "Well, the roads are dry enough now. We're not going to have any more severe weather and so forth. Let's get that salvage out of there." So these two men went out, one with a power-saw and one with a tractor. Through the year, Marv in his travels, and I in my travels, would spot all these dead trees, downed trees. Sometimes in two weeks we would have it all cleaned up. But we picked every tree, every one. And I go out and look at the national forests and some of those places with those trees, salvage trees, dead trees, downed trees, everything else, rotting, you know, and I think they should be doing the same thing. They say; "Oh, we can't do it. It isn't economically feasible. But, by golly, it is! I know it is!
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, you've had a long career. Is there anything that stands out in your mind that you're most satisfied about?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, some of the things that stand out in my mind as being the most interesting, I guess, is 56 or 57 years ago, my first job in the woods. I was 14 years old, just got out of grammar school. Didn't have any child labor laws then. I got a job working and punking whistles in a logging camp. It was a small operation and a truck logging operation. That was 1920; I was 14, I remember; born in 1908. What's eight and fourteen? 1922. On a truck logging outfit. I can remember those old trucks. They were straight up and down, and
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Macs. They didn't have any brakes on the front wheels, no brakes on the trailers, and we didn't have any tractors and bulldozers in those days. We built a road across a wet place and planked it. The history of logging says truck logging first began in 1923. Well, I worked on one in 1922, O I know it started before then.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You started with truck logging then?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that was the first year, I think, that they did truck logging. That's one of the interesting parts of my life. And then another thing that I always thought put me in good stead in my teaching is the variety that I had. I worked every summer in logging camps then. I punked whistles, I set chokers, I felled timber and got banged up in camp, and everything else, and then I worked for private surveyors. I worked for the forest service for quite a few years. I worked for Weyerhaeuser for six or seven years, doing a variety of things, and then I came here to the university.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the last dean you worked with was Dean Stoltenberg?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you retired?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right, I worked for three deans.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you didn t know Peavy?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I knew him, but I didn't work with him. He was around for the first couple of years that I was here. He was around the building a lot - in the old building, you know - because he'd come in just to visit. He was looking for more timber land for Paul Dunn. Paul wanted to build that up to 20,000 acres, that timber land; thought we needed that much for a school forest. But Mac got in. He decided that we didn't need any more land; there were too many problems taking care of it.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How do you feel about that now? Do you think we should have gotten more?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, I was with Paul all along. I argued with Mac, and Mac said, "We cannot justify to the public, to the State of Oregon, taking more land out of taxes unless we absolutely need it." But see, we're putting more money back in there than they'd ever get in taxes. Oh, yes, that was a crime they didn't get more land. Gosh, we could have gotten itso cheaply then, even if they got it cheaply then and sold it now.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How was Carl Stoltenberg? Did he support the McDonald Forest activities from the dean's office?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, quite a bit. Of course, Carl's whole experience had been in spending money and not making money. I know he told me several times when I had this account built up... 1 ran the thing like a business, sort of; I didn't blow the money just because it came in. But he said, "We're not in the business of making money; we're in the business of spending money."
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you get along well with him?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, we had our differences, but Carl is a politician. He is pretty easy to get along with. He gets his own way at the end. (chuckle)
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Finally, how would you compare the forest now with the way it was when you took over in 1959?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it looks more like a managed forest now instead of just a neglected forest. I think there's more timber volume on it now than there was then. They have been cutting 3 to 5 million every year and increasing the volume.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think Marv Rowley has done a good job, then, of managing?
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, of course I haven't been out there for three or four years. I don't know now. I think there is more timber volume on that forest now than if we hadn't done any cutting.
entries.chapter_ref: I.16 Forest Management and Hiring Marvin Rowley

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: PART II

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: SEPTEMBER 18, 1979 INTERVIEW

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: (Interview conducted by Royal Jackson at Peavy Hall, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon)

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. OAK CREEK

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What we've done here, Bill, is Marv Rowley has sat down with me and marked, in red, all the places he knows about in McDonald Forest: trails, cabins, old sawmill sites. We've systematically gone out and visited all of these. What I thought I'd try to find out from you is information on, for example, Oak Creek Guard Station. Do you know anything about that old homestead that's just a little bit up from the guard station?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything there in the days that you managed the forest?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was all gone by the time that I came here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you came here when?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you never did see a building of any kind there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about the Oak Creek Guard Station? If you came in 1946, that was completed by then, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who was living there at that time, do you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember the fellow's name, but somebody that worked at the lab. He was not on the faculty; he was a civil service employee.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he a caretaker?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he wasn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He didn't keep a key to the gate or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He probably did. I think he did some maintenance out there, but he primarily just worked at the lab. Then they moved him out to the Jackson place. Then Ray Yoder lived there quite a while, and then Lloyd Hayes; they were on the faculty.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was after 1946?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up until the time it ceased to be a residence and became a research facilily?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think it was vacant there for a while after that. Nobody wanted to live there on the faculty, I guess. McCulloch was dean, I think, when they rented it to the fisheries department. Chuck Dane was assistant dean. He handled the thing; it was his idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Chuck Dane was Assistant Dean of Forestry?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He is on the business staff now. I think he is head of one of the departments over there. He was, last year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the idea of renting it to the Fisheries and WiMlfe Department? Just to be cooperative?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just to be cooperative, I guess. I didn't like the idea at all, but I wasn't consulted much even though I was forest manager. I thought that if we started making enough money on the forest, which we soon did, it would be an excellent place to house a kind of head maintenance man, or something for the forest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That idea didn 't prevail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they went ahead and turned it over to the fisheries department. The fisheries department rented it, in fact.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think the fisheries department still does rent it for a dollar a year, or something like that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was more than that. And we also rented quite a few acres of land to them, at our estimated income from that land, because they didn't want it touched. Some of the purest water they'd found in Oregon came down off the hill there; that goes across the road just north of it. So we stayed out of that watershed except when the wind blew some trees down up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've not logged or meddled in that area at all, maybe since 1951?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, let's see, it was later than that. It would be in the fifties, I suppose; I don't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What structures do you remember at the Oak Creek Guard Station site? For instance, what they call the Horse Barn, was that there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the main residence?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the residence, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything else there that you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the Horse Barn used for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nothing, I guess. They may have stored something there, but I'm not sure. But I don't remember it being used for anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you were the manager, you didn't use it for anything? You didn 't store equipment there, or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any particular problems associated with that entry to the forest, trespassing, or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no more than the other entries. We had problems with all of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Illegal entry?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because they weren't supposed to be in there and they wanted to go in. They'd find some way to get around it. I think maybe less problems there than some of the ones way off where nobody was around, where they could tear the gates down to get in, pull the fences down, and that sort of thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You don't remember anything at all, then, about this old homestead site that was just above the Guard Station?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I know there were some apple trees there, and that's about all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had you heard any stories about what might have happened there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Aren't there remnants of an orchard around the Oak Creek Guard Station, that look like a previous site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, just by the gate. You see, the gate is inside of our property line now, past that house where there is so much traffic to the fisheries. We put the gate beyond it, and right there's an apple tree. When we stopped to unlock the gate the students would jump off the truck and go and grab apples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Grab an apple off the tree, on the run?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but as I told you before, a strange thing happened. One day we were up here; I had the seniors out on a survey crew, or something. There's a great big old sawmill site, just a big blackberry patch...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: At the junction of Road 6020 and 600?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's just above there. Great big blackberry patch that came in on the old sawdust pile, I guess, where the sawmill was. I was telling this one student, "There used to be a sawmill there," and he said, "Yes, I know, my grandfather was a sawyer in that mill."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but there's a town northwest of here named after his family. I can't remember his name. I thought it was kind of funny; I thought I was telling him something he didn't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the mill that was located right at the junction of Road 6020 and 600, right in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's right above it; It's above the junction about 100 or 200 feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right on the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the left side of the road; It's between the road and the creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: As you are going north, it's on the left side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the old OS. U. school sawmill? What do you remember about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, quite a bit, I guess. We got that surplus property from the federal government.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mean the sawmill and equipment?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All the equipment, yes. And the products department wanted it, forest products, to demonstrate cutting lumber and what not. But we had a fellow on the forest engineering faculty who was a captain in the Army during the war, and he was in charge of a forestry company in France that was cutting lumber for the war effort. They had a mill just like that, and he was in charge of it, so he knew a lot about it. His name was Ralph DeMoisy. He put the mill together, with the help of students, and then the products department took it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And did they operate every day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, sporadically, when they could get it to run.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was kind of hard to keep running?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they finally got another engine for it, but somebody on the forest products faculty was in charge, who had never had much experience with a sawmill - most of their experience was in schools. It didn't work out vety well. The forest engineering department undertook to log for them, get logs down there. Finally, they got so many logs down there, they about covered the mill up. They ran it for quite a while and were losing money right along. So Dean McCulloch finally decided that it was a losing proposition, and wasn't worth it. He was worried about students getting hurt with the saws and what not, safety factor. So he just sold it to Alaska Junk, and they hauled it away

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the building that housed it, was it torn down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think part of it is still there, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, there's nothing left at all.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somebody probably hauled all the lumber off. The foundation was there, and the platform was all there, and the planks. I imagine people have hauled it off. The lumber was worth a lot of money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the usual routine there? How would the day open up f it was running? Would the sawyer come and get it started, then the students?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think they'd just go out in a truck. They'd all go out there and start it running. The students ran it under the supervision of the faculty. I think Jim Snodgrass did most of the on-the-job supervision there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he a faculty member?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, in products, and Jack Grantham, who was head of the department at that time, was in charge of it. But they could only cut 2 or 3,000 board feet a day, I think. They'd have five, or six, or seven people around there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A lot of breakdowns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, a lot of breakdowns.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The idea was to give the students practical experience?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Practical experience, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the mill typical of those being used in the industry at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was built for the Army. Now, you know the things that the Army does take a lot of manpower, and a lot of money to run. Anything they do, I guess. So they had to have quite a few men. It was pretty much hand labor: pulling lumber around, and pushing it through, and pulling it off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is it accurate to say it was antiquated when the school got it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as far as being efficient for a commercial operation, it wasn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The industry had already advanced beyond this type of a sawmill, so the students weren't really learning much that they could apply?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, only fundamentals, you know, sawing lumber, and some of the problems, and so forth. But nothing was automated, it was all hand labor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I heard there were some contests, at times, where the F. E. 's would bring the timber, and the F. P's would saw it up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't any contest. One time Snodgrass was talking to a group of faculty or someone, said one of the reasons we haven't been able to cut more out there is that we have been short of logs. We had some older forest engineering students working out there, veterans from the wax. They had an old beat-up truck and they used a grader to roll the logs on. That kind of teed them off so they covered that dang mill up with logs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They took that as a challenge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, time goes by so fast. At least 15 years ago, between 15 and 20 years. But when they decided to shut the mill down, we had a lot of logs there. Finally - I don't know whether Marv did that after he started logging for us or not - but they were hauled out and sold to some mill here in town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this flume that is shown coming down to the sawmill at the junction of Road 6020? Did you ever see that fiwne?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I saw parts of it up there all decayed, of course, way up the creek here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's up the west fork of the Oak Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up in here, around the old sawmill. There's still some iron gears and stuff still up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marv and I found that. It's still there: a lot offire brick, stacks of broken fire brick

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was the dangdest mess of brick down here - way down in the bottom - and was going to go down and get that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, you're talking about down in the bottom of the canyon of the west fork of Oak Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: See this loop it makes around, right in there? I was running a survey line through there one day and ran across the brick. I thought I would carry the brick out of that canyon sometime. The old-timers told me that years ago they used to flume that lumber to Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did it go? From Oak Creelç, and then where?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know where it ended up; I don't know if it went clear into town or not. It gets pretty flat down there. They don't need much drop, there's plenty of drop from there on down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there enough water in Oak Creek to flume that timber down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes. What they used to do in the fluming business - I don't know if they did here or not - if there wasn't enough water they'd put in a dam up there, let the dam get full, and then they'd open it up, then plug it up again, and build up some more water. But there's quite a bit of water in Oak Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you saw these rotting pieces of the flume, were they long lengths ofjust little tiny support beams, or what?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there were some support beams and some rotted timbers that they used, so that you could see it was a flume.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year would that have been, roughly? Or even, what decade?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That I saw it? Probably 25 years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's completely gone now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You don't see it any more?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, Marv and I walked all over this area, and he found what he thought might have been a piece here and there, but it was indistinguishable.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Up above here, I saw it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You saw it much closer to the sawmill? We walked that whole area there. Did you ever know anyone that worked on the sawmill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know if the fellow that was a sawyer here was from the same outfit, I suppose, around the same time. Maybe he worked there, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marv thinks that this sawmill operated around 1910 or 1920, but he's not sure. Does that sound reasonable to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, probably. You see, that was all horse-logged in there. That's why they didn't get back in very far, didn't get in the steeper ground, and didn't cut too much for the horses to get out. There's probably more sawmill sites that we don't know about there, because they didn't want to go very far with the horses and bring it to the sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the old homestead on Homestead Road? Did you ever know anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, except that there was one there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever see the building?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The orchard? Or did you ever know anybody that lived there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did you know there was a homestead there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Evidences, and the old road in there. There was a very steep road - and they hail to straighten it out afterwards - and there was a building up there, at the top. Has Marv got this road open now?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, you can drive right up into here; it ends somewhere in here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a tremendously steep road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Homestead Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Going in there, yes. And there are some old buildings in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that must be the homestead on Homestead Road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I remember that now. I remember that very, very steep road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because I remember Marv and I went up there one day and we looked around here, tried to get a road back in here to get some of this timber out here, dead stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's up above Homestead Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we went up here where the little road turns off and there's a little flat right there where the buildings were. They may have burned the buildings.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's go back over here to the sawmill site, right off the Road 600. Do you know anything about this sawmill site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, except that there's one there, I guess.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever see it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you never did see anything there at all, just knew there was some sawdust there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember - I've seen so many of those old homesteads, with sawdust piles, and what not around the forest - I don't remember what that one looked like at all. I just recall this one here because of the steep road and the flat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up on Homestead Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I remember some kind of an orchard there. Seems to me there was even a walnut tree there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this O.S. U. weather radar site that atmospheric sciences put up? What do you remember about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Fred Decker... do you know Fred?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He knows all about it. He set it up, and he got some money from the Navy, and the thing kind of fell through, and it was vandalized pretty heavily. They stole anything that was any good up there; went in on motorcycles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Whose responsibility was it to clean up the remains of that site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose it was the atmospheric science department. They were the ones that were fussing with it. It was sure a mess the last time I saw it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: McCulloch simply gave them permission to do that? Was that in writing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gosh, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You never did see any kind of an agreement?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, well you know, this was university property and so there didn't need to be too much of a contract, not between departments. And then I think it was Fred Decker, I'm not sure, that named that McCulloch Peak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He said he did. That peak didn't really have a name.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it didn't. And I think he named it McCulloch Peak. He got into a lot of trouble with the right-of-way up there. Did he tell you about that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this road that goes up there... Where the heck does it take off? Down here some place? Here it goes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, up Alder Creek? That road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, now there's a guy that lives there, owns this property. He did work for the university. He is the most cantankerous guy, and I can't remember his name right now. He didn't want anybody on his property or on that road. Starker had a right-of-way across it, I guess, but that's all. He just wouldn't let anybody up there. He took a shot at a Boy Scout once that was walking through there. Up here now, there was a fence; this was all fenced at one time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You're talking about the southwestern-most boundary of the fore st?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We went out here some place, this road; We were thinning out in there, and one tree fell over and hit the fence; it kind of broke it down. Well, this guy wrote me the nastiest letter about knocking down his fence - it wasn't his fence at all, the school built it - and cutting those trees. He says, "I assume now since you did that I can go in and cut all the wood I want for myself on the school property, and I assume you are going to fix that fence immediately," and so forth. So I talked to Marv - Marv was doing the logging. He said, "I'm not going to fix his fence." I wrote the fellow a nice letter and told him that fence belonged to the school. The school had built it, and our tree had knocked it down, and we would certainly repair it. We let it go at that and never heard any more from him. Old Fred Decker had a hell-of-a-time getting a right-of-way through there, so Fred talked to me one time and we were just about to build a road around to it. We got one around there now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and so we wouldn't have to go through there. But, the thing is, Marv's cat driver got too ambitious and he built the damn thing on through. After this was gone, I wanted to stop here so people couldn't come - you can get in there easy from other roads, you can get in here and get into the forest - so Marv had him go up there and put in a big pile of dirt there. So you go up to find that four-wheel drivers had cleared the dirt off so they could get in; they sure find out how to get into the forest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marv said he thought there was an old trail off Road 600 going toward Road 680. Afoot trail goes out across the hill here to Woods Creek, and a trail to Price Creek. Did you ever see this trail? The red dotted line taking off of Road 600 going toward 680?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only trail that I know of, that was usable - we used to keep it open - comes around here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: By Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not Sulphur Springs, Lewisburg Saddle. It came around here. I said to the students, "Go out and clear the danged thing." People like to walk through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did it terminate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It terminated here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Clear over to Road 600?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it crossed a little foot bridge here. It's probably still there, and then it cut across and it cut just into Starker's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Across the corner of Starker's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, around here, down here. It went some place right in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marv thought that was a CCC [Civilian Conservation Corps] trail. Does that make sense to you?
bracketed_corrections: [Civilian Conservation Corps]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably built by the CCC's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For what purpose?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, for biking, I suppose. See, they had the CCC camp down at Peavy Arboretum.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, Camp Arboretum.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And they built this house here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oak Creek Guard Station?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and they did a lot of work on roads, and so forth, and trails - mostly trails - and worked around the nursery down there. So they probably built that trail. You could probably still see it along here. Of course, up in here, Starker logged that; obliterated that part of it.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2. MCDONALD FOREST ACQUISITION

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's the history of Starker owning this piece here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you hear all kinds of stories about it. When Mrs. McDonald told Dean Peavy that she'd like to do something for the school, because her husband had made a lot of money in lumbering in Oregon, and Peavy told her the best thing she could do, what the school most needed, was a forest lab near the school so they could get to it easily. And she said, "Fine. Whenever you find property that's reasonable, that you want, contact my attorney, and he will make the money available for you." So Peavy was picking up a piece at a time, a piece at a time all through here; anything that was cheap, you know, a couple of dollars an acre. And he was dickering for this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For the piece that Starker now owns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because it was right in the middle. Starker knew about it, of course, and he jumped in and beat them to it and bought it for himself. And he was on the faculty here at the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that make some people mad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, I wasn't here at that time Starker bought that piece while he was on the faculty, but that's the story I heard; I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the school ever try to buy it from him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he didn't want to sell. One time Starker approached Dean Dunn - that was before I was manager of the forest, when Harry Nettleton was manager. The school had 160 acres, still had, on Mary's Peak - the Spaulding Tract - about 60 percent of it covered with beautiful second-growth timber. So when Starker had that logged he came to Paul Dunn and said, "Now Paul, I'll trade you this 360 acres even up for your 160; I'm willing to do that for the school." Whenever Starker says something like that, you watch out. (laughter) So Paul Dunn asked Harry Nettleton to evaluate the two pieces, and he just about had Paul convinced that he should trade. So Nettleton told Paul, "Why don't you get Bill Davies to evaluate that because that was his field. He's done a lot of that for Weyerhaeuser, and so forth." So I agreed to do it. George Barnes had made a cru se of the 160 acres up there and had all the data on it. The timber on the Spaulding Tract on Mary's Peak was worth two or three times as much, I think. But Starker came back in to see Paul about the deal; he was mad. T. J. owned some stuff right next to that on Mary's Peak so it would have been an excellent piece of property for him. But with my estimate, Paul backed off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year was that roughly, do you know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, it's probably in the Spaulding Tract files.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe in the fifties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably in the fifties. It was before I became manager of the forest, and I think I became manager in 1959. So it was probably around 1950.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bill, looking at the western half of McDonald Forest, are there sites you know about that haven't been marked on here which we should indicate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But then to finish that story, Paul offered to buy it on Bill Davies' estimate of the value and Starker said, "Well, no, I'd rather have the property than the money." I always assumed that it's in T. J.'s will, I don't know, or maybe he has turned it over to the boys. One of the boys was in several years ago about things out here. They were going to do something with it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the school gave up trying to secure that particular inholding?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they hope they'll get it somehow. It's right in the middle of the forest. We ought to have it, Jimminy Christmas. Not too much value to anybody else now; cut all the timber off it. It'll be maybe 20 to 30 years before they can harvest any more off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any other sites in this general area that we haven't marked that you know about: sawmill sites, homesteads, trails, anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This little piece in here. It's got the original old-growth timber in it because the timber wasn't much good anyway, it was just big. They used that for the students' use; they looked at it to study defective timber. A lot of defective timber in there; very typical spot for a place that's going bad, that's deteriorating. The fir is the old growth that's rotting, and the other stuff is coming in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're talking about just below and south of Starker's holding?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right where that trail takes off. The trail takes off of Road 600, and it's right in the trail, goes right through it, that little piece right in there. Mostly before you get to the creek and back up the hill; not over the line because that's all cut. But that's right on the road there, and a lot of people never get out to see timber and they enjoy seeing those big trees in there. I got hell from some of the people in the botany department. Inside the loop here

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: there were three or four great big trees, and they were dying - one of them died, it was a snag, and afraid it would fall down, and two or three others in there - so we just cut them and took them out and got some new timber started. I got hell for that. We left this alone; it's a heck of a waste of money, but maybe it's worth it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a lot of old growth still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, quite a bit of money could be salvaged out of it right now. In a 100 years it'll probably be gone, and you can't get anything out of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: East of Road 600?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That sharp switchback there, right off to the left as you go around that switchback, if you're going up the switchback. If you ever go out there again, look in there. Somebody on your faculty, about five years ago, went on a trip up there - had a show-me trip for the faculty - and he made a little talk about the cathedral-type trees up there. Beautiful, (laughter) rotten trees with conks all over them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Called them cathedral trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, who was that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Mike Freed is who it sounds like.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was, I think, yes.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 3. JACKSON PLACE

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about this area here, Bill (talking about Road 620 near the Jackson Place)? We have shelters built by CCC's. Marv indicated Road 612.4, does that ring a bell to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that's where the Red Hats used to have some activities. You know about the Red Hats? They had some activities in there, and I think the Boy Scouts used to go up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What shelters were there, do you know? What did they look like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I think they were just open-faced. If you've been back in there you have probably seen them. On a trail way back in there, shelters, open shelters, closed on three sides, open on the other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any out there now? I haven't seen any shelters out there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We may have burned them. They were getting decrepit, and kids were going out there, hiking out in there, and fussing with them. We were afraid they were going to burn down. But right up there on the south side of the creek, you go across the bridge there, there's kind of a meadow, you go back on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Jackson Place. Did you ever know anybody named Jackson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they got that, I think, when Peavy was buying up the land with Mrs. McDonald's money. The school spent some money fixing up this old house that was on there when they moved this guy out of Oak Creek Station; I don't see why they were obligated to furnish him a house. This was a fellow that worked at the lab. I would remember his name if I heard it. But he wasn't on the faculty; he was civil service, a mechanic, or something down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anyway, they moved him into the Jackson house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and they spent some money fixing it up. And moved Yoder or Lloyd Hayes, whichever came first, in there [Oak Creek]. This fellow at Jackson Place - I don't know if he still lives there - he teaches; I think he is or was a track coach at Crescent Valley High School. He bought a piece of property right here he's going to build on and he rented this house. He just loves that place out there; he's got some horses he runs around out there, you know.
bracketed_corrections: [Oak Creek]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still lives on the Jackson Place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Did when I retired six years ago. He used to call me up and say, "Something is wrong. The roof is leaking on one side," he says, "you know, I'll re-roof that thing if you'll buy the roofing." So we bought the roofing and he re-roofed it. He didn't pay much rent, but he paid some. And he'd paint the place if we'd buy the paint, and that sort of thing. He was a heck-of-a good tenant. And he kept people from vandalizing stuff around there; he'd see that the gate was kept locked. He may still be there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about this orchard that's marked there, right down below 612.2? Did you ever know anything about that, right below the Jackson house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember anything about it. That's over on the south side of the creek. There's an opening, kind of a meadow over there. This fellow's horses, I've seen them in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this "Orchard, possible homesite" that Marv has marked along Road 612? Have you ever seen anything there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I've seen an orchard; there's lots of trees. You know, there are trees right along the north side of Jackson Creek; they're right by the road where this road turns off here. A pear tree right in there - I used to pick pears off it - and then there's apples, pears all along in here. I don't remember over here. And I remember that opening over there; never saw any fruit trees of any kind in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's move up a little higher on the map now, right off Sulphur Springs Road. He's got an old sawmill site mentioned, on "An old pioneer road." Do you know anything about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, except there was an old road in there. Hard to find it now, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever see any sawdust at this site?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not that I remember.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 4. PEAVY'S CABIN

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He's got the CCC trail running from Peavy 's cabin over here connecting up with this trail that you mentioned. That starts at this bend in Road 600. Do you remember any of this trail that runs from Lewisburg Saddle up to Peavy's cabin? Is that part of the same system?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably is, but see, they built this road up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which one, the Nettleton Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but they probably followed the trail. I don't remember the trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Peavy 's cabin, now that was falling down when you were manager, wasn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you had it completely burned down or taken down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Taken down. We did burn afterward. I think they cut a lot up for wood or something; took it down to the Forestry Club Cabin. We were afraid of fire there, also. Nobody was using it much, and the logs were getting all rotten and bugs in them, and kids would climb up the hill and build fires in the fireplaces. We were afraid they would burn it down so I talked to Dean McCulloch about it. Some of the people who had built the cabin for Peavy were still alive and he contacted some of them and told them what we thought we ought to do, and they said they thought that would be a good thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just dismantle it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Make a memorial to Peavy out of it because Peavy loved that cabin. I had a concrete slab poured there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was no floor there before that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wood floor, just like a house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you had the concrete slab poured in the exact location of the foundation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I believe they had a concrete foundation, so I had this slab poured, which would be permanent, and we kept the fireplace. We had to do some work on it. Had a plaque there and somebody stole the plaque; and there were a lot of nice agates and things in the original fireplace, and the kids would come up there and chip them out, stole them. We were going to plug the thing - I don't know if we ever got around to it or not - because kids still went up there and built fires, and we were afraid of fires again; we were going to close the fireplace off and put a sheet of metal and concrete in it, or something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It still looks like it's a functional fireplace. How about that radio antenna? Was it there when the cabin was torn down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. It occurred about the same time though, I remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's on school land, isn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who gave permission for that to be placed there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we did, through the dean. The dean and I decided that we shouldn't fight it, it's university property. We leased the property, and the State Board of Higher Education, the chancellor approached us about it. If we'd said no, they'd probably done it anyway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was the educational channel?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they wanted it, and we thought it was a good idea, and the people that were in charge of that here at the university were very cooperative, always cooperative.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's their access point, Lewisburg Saddle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lewisburg Saddle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Has that ever been a problem in management in the years that you worked there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not with the people over there; they were very, very cooperative. No problem. In fact, we liked to have them out there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To help you watch it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, watch it. They had a key - we finally gave them a key - I think to Lewisburg Saddle and on down at the other end at Peavy Arboretum in case we got snow in there sometime and couldn't get up there. So we'd take the cat, Marv's cat, and go up there and clean the snow out so they could go up there, and they appreciated that. They see anything going on up there they'd always call me. Some hippies from California wanted to move into the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Forestry Club Cabin one time and they alerted us on that. If they'd have gotten in there, you know, you can't get them out very easy. So we liked to have them up there.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that actually happen, that the hippies moved into the cabin?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they didn't. But they hiked up there - they'd heard about it - they hiked up from Lewisburg Saddle.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was Peavy's Cabin or the Forestry Club Cabin?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know which one they were going to move into, but they came up there and wanted to know where this cabin was; they asked the fellow that was up there. It may have been just after we burned the other one down. He told them this was a closed area, private, and the gates were locked, and they couldn't do that. Never heard anymore about it, but they'd heard about that Forestry Club Cabin and were about to move their commune right into it. They get in there and established, you know, you're an old meany if you run them out.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was the KOAC people that helped you on that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, they were a big help, they were up there. I talked to them a lot, and they said they'd keep watch for fires. They had a telephone there at that place - that was the only telephone they had on the forest - and they wanted to give me a key to the place to get in so that I could use the phone. But I refused to accept it because I might have been suspect if somebody had broken in there and stole things, and so forth; and so I didn't want a key to a lot of valuable equipment.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, they keep it manned, don't they? Or just during the day?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's manned whenever they're broadcasting. I guess that's most of the time now.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Daily, Ithink
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they didn't broadcast all the time when they first put it in.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No one stays overnight, do they? There isn't a permanent resident there? Did they put the road in that goes up to that tower? Road 5010?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, there was a road right up there to Peavy's Cabin, right along side of Peavy's Cabin.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That road was already there?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we may have improved it for them a little bit, I don't remember.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 5. FIELD TRIPS TO MCDONALD FOREST
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marv's got this "Harwood Spring: old hunting cabin" marked. What do you know about that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a favorite place of Harry Patterson, whom I replaced as Head of the Forest Engineering Department. He'd always take his senior crew out there on field trips and show them that spring, which is wonderful water. They all had to go down and have a drink out of that spring.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's called Harwood Spring?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I always wanted to change the name. There's another spring down there we always called Patterson Springs. That was another place he'd take the students to get a drink of water. I don't remember just where it was. I imagine Marv would know. You see, Marv was a student of Pat's, and you can ask Marv about that. Patterson Springs, I used to call it that. It's just off the road there, we could walk down to it right in there, just below the road, the main road.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tell me about Harwood Springs. How did it get its name?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't any idea.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a cabin there? What's that old hunting cabin Marv's got listed?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was an old cabin there at one time, I think, but it's gone now.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right on the springs, right by it?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Near there.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You don't know who built it?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But Patterson liked to take his people down there to get water? Why do you think he thought that was so good?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, he used to have a place out there where he'd take the students to practice running curves on the roads. He'd always go down there and get water out of the springs.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one you call Patterson Springs?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At noon, yes, and they'd boil up coffee. Pat always made coffee in a great big old black coffee pot. They used to kid Pat about his strong coffee, and said the way he made coffee was to put some boiling water on and put a rock in it and keep putting coffee in until the rock came to the top, then the coffee was ready. (laughter)
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mean on afield trip he'd make coffee?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they had eight-hour labs in those days.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The students brought their own lunches?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They brought their own lunch. And about 11:30 a.m. Pat would assign one of the students - that was a big ritual with him there - to go over and get the pot, and build a fire, and get ready to put the coffee on. Pat would usually make the coffee, and they'd sit around the lunch fire and talk about their work. Actually, I think more instruction went on around that danged lunch fire than in the classroom.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The students felt like they were really learning?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they were relaxed, you know. I used to do the same thing a lot of times, when we had six-hour labs. In fact, somebody from the Oregonian got wise to it and came down and did a big two-page spread for the Sunday Oregonian on it one time.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'd like to go look that article up. Do you have any idea where I'd start looking, what year?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gosh no, I don't remember; I think it was the Oregonian. It was kind of a glamorized deal. They even took a girl out there and took a picture of her on the road. They took some pictures of us sitting around the campfire, and me talking to the students, and students running lines with the transit, and things like that. It was a long time ago.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Fifties?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fifties or sixties, or something like that.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You wouldn't have a clipping of that article at home, would you?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably not, my wife throws all that stuff away.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's a shame, should have kept it.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but I don't remember who it was that did it. I think it was a graduate student or a senior in journalism here, and he did that for one of his projects or something. If it got published in the paper, then you got a double "A", or something, but he got that published.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was done through the journalism department probably?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, well Pat used to go down to that spring and get water, and I always called that Patterson Springs.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Evidently the name didn 't stick; there's nothing marked on here called Patterson Springs.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I'm the only one who ever called it that.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about this right here, "Oak felled along these foothills to feed livestock during the winter of 1883"? Did you ever see the stumps or logs, or anything that was left from that period?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, out in the Dunn Forest there's another place where they did that. I could see the old logs and stumps down there. Funny thing, they had a sign on one of them saying just that. There was a trail out here from the Forestry Club Cabin.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, here's the Pine Race Trail, is that...
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where's the Forestry Club Cabin?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Here's Memorial Grove; here's Cronemiller Lake; there's the Forestry Cabin, right here.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, this trail. Now there was a stump right in here some place.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The trail leading from the Forestry Cabin...
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Went right by that stump and there was a sign on it; somebody put a sign there, "Felled in 18", whatever it was.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who would put that up, do you know?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, somebody on the faculty here, I suppose. When we thinned in there, one of the loggers, on one of the stumps that we cut, took some cardboard and he made a sign there, "Felled in 1950 or 1960", whatever it was, "to feed loggers". (laughter)
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A little logger humor, huh? How about this early fire lookout? Did you ever see that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What's this?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Looks like a radio antenna, Marv wrote that. Did you ever see that fire lookout? Marv said it was up in a tree.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember that. I remember the antenna because that's when they had the state forestry department's division here. And they moved it later to Philomath, but they had their offices here.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: By here, you mean at the Nursery?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, by the Nursery, where the Peavy Lodge is now, that was state forestry, and they had that up there for radio communication.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that lookout, who put that up there? Did you ever see it?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, no.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear about it?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think I did, something about it. But it wasn't there when I came.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marv claims he's seen something in a tree up there: a lookout, a little plaiform or something.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Could be, maybe I just thought it was a little platform to get at the antenna. They had just a straight, tall antenna going out of the tree there.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He's got an archeological site listed here. Did you ever see anything like that? Like Indian arrowheads or anything like that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this trail is still in use. You know that trail there, I had that cleaned out several times.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, that's a trail that runs from Road 500 northeasterly up to intake lake pipeline. Was that a CCC trail originally?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably, it goes down to the lake.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who put this plaque up there? I think it's a plaque to Schreiner, isn't it?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Fred Schreiner Road. I don't know, that was put up before I came here. I put the ones up on Nettleton Road. I don't know if they're still there or not.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There is a sign on Nettleton Road, and one for Patterson Road.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Patterson... Let's see, which one is Patterson?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Farther down, over here on the western part of the forest.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that's right, Patterson. Patterson goes to here; and Nettleton goes from here down to the Powder House.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any other sites in the eastern part of McDonald Forest that we don't have marked that you know about?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. I think they'd been moved out. The foundations and what-not were there, but I think they were moved out.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That came in with the Adair Tract, didn't it?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it was a little different contract, but it came about the same time.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about T. J. 's post farm there, what do you remember about that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I remember it was carried on for a long time. It was put in long before I came here. T. J. put that in to study about the posts - how long they would last in the ground, things like that - so people could tell the farmers, "If you make a fence out of such-and-such posts it'll rot off in seventeen years," or whatever. And it was kept going after T. J. left here for quite a while, and I think it was disbanded a long time ago.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not operating now?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this building site off the 541 Road that Marv has marked, do you know anything about that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see, where are we now?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cronemiller Lake, just north and east of Cronemiller Lake.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nope.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You do remember this sawmill site that's at the end?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because that was the only sawdust pile from the old sawmills out there that I know of that didn't cover up with brush or blackberries. This sawdust was still there and it was black, and you could take your hand and squeeze it into a ball like clay.
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why was that?
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know why. It was full of mushrooms. I used to take Dean McCulloch out there - once a year was all I could get him on the forest - take a lunch and go all day. We'd show him what we had done during the year and what we planned to do, and all that sort of thing. And when we got this road opened here and we got this property, I said, "Mac, I want to show you the best sawdust pile in the state of Oregon." I said, "You could sell that and make a lot of money, for mulch." I had a pickup that we had bought with school
entries.chapter_ref: II.5 Field Trips to McDonald Forest

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: money, so we were in the pickup; we always carried a shovel along, too, in case of fire. He said, "Well, I'd like to have some of that for around my flowers at home." And I said, "Well, let's get some." So we drove over there and filled the pickup with that sawdust and hauled it home and shoveled it out in his yard. Last time I was up there it was all gone. Other people had found out about it, you know, and boy they flocked in; faculty, they thought that was wonderful sawdust.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I heard that Vern McDaniels hauled sawdust for the nursery from there. Did you ever hear that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maybe he did later, after he found out about it. But nobody had taken much out of it at that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right up from there is this place called "Old Pigpen Road." Marv Rowley called it that. Did you ever see any pigpens in there? I think that's the name the loggers gave it when they were operating there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's old roads all grown up in there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 6. THE BLAKE HOUSE

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the Blake House is right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I got in trouble; I didn't get in trouble, but I got a lot of dirty looks for that. I had that burned down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did you do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we rented it for quite a while - we got the property, and the Blakes moved out and everything - and we never could get any satisfactory renters. They'd live in it for a while and then they'd move out and leave it all a mess. When they got started moving people in the old Adair, all the kids would come over and they had a hey-day in it. They broke all the windows out of it, and I could see where they'd had a fire in it. Luckily it went out before it got too far. So I told the dean, I'm going to burn the danged house down before we get in trouble. Somebody found out about it. Some woman in town said, "That's an old historical landmark. You can't burn it down." I said, "Well, it's going to get burned sooner or later, those kids playing with matches in it. It's deteriorating; it is an eyesore now, all the windows broken out; they've broken the doors down, and they are hanging loose; and they've stolen stuff, they've taken everything of any value; and they've stole all the door knobs, stole everything out of it."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a two story house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, nice, old mansion-looking house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many rooms in it, do you know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gee, I don't know. There were quite a few of them, eight or ten. Big two story, raised a family in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever know Blake?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, when I first came here. He was 80 then, I guess. So I called up the fire department out there, the Adair Army fire crew. The weather had been rainy. I said, "How would you like to get some fire practice?" They said, "That's fine, we'll burn that doggone thing down". "Be sure you burn everything up." So they went Out there and burned it all up for me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was that, do you know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, that must have been 20 years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there much of an uproar over you doing it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't hear much. They realized that the danged thing was an eyesore. This woman proposed that it be made a park there around the building, and the house be restored and kept restored. Now, who's going to keep it restored? And she said, "Can't you do that?" And I said, "No, we can't do that. You'd have to have somebody there 24 hours a day, 365 days a year because one day you go away and the kids would have it down again." And she said, "Maybe the county could do it." I think I called the county, or she did, or something, and they didn't want to do it. We figured the best thing to do was burn it down because it was looking worse and worse all the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's some legend about those two black locust trees. What had you heard about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Blake told me personally about those.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did he tell you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we were up there when we were dickering about buying the 40 back in there from him. He was talking about the old days, and he said the old Portland-Umpqua Valley Highway went this side of his house, right through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cut across there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he was telling me stories about that, in the early years when he was just a little guy. He said one day two girls came riding through there on horses. They had these locust whips for their horses and they stuck them in the ground. Then I guess his folks or his wife, whoever was there with him, invited them in for tea or something, like they always did in those days. And when they left they forgot their whips - they didn't take them with them - and they sprouted and grew. That's his story.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is it reasonable to assume that it could happen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, most of the hardwoods will sprout - willows, maples. You know, McCulloch swears that these gate posts down here at the entry way to Peavy Arboretum - the two maples there on either side of the road that goes in - he claims that those were gate posts that sprouted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he see them when they were planted?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so. That would be a long time ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But a lot of these stories get passed on from one person to the next, and there's not much basis of fact.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, one time my high school teacher, to prove that, whispered a story to the first guy in the class and had him whisper it all the way around, and then the last guy told the story and it was entirely different, absolutely different. But Blake also told me that one day they had the Umpqua Indians down there where some of them got on the war path, so they were going to transfer them up to the Grand Ronde Reservation. And the Army officers and these renegade Indians came up the road there and they stopped and asked the Blakes if they could have some water for the horses and men. He said he remembered that vividly - taking the Indians past his house.

entries.speaker: Q
